summaries.gardner: Southern Copper is the opposite of a Rule Breaker: a mature, cyclical commodity miner controlled by Grupo Mexico, with no consumer brand and no disruptive product. It does score on strong recent price momentum and on analysts calling it overvalued, but it lacks the innovation, visionary leadership and emerging-industry leadership Gardner looks for.
summaries.buffett: It has a durable cost advantage from what it says are the world's largest copper reserves and earns high returns, but it sells a commodity with no pricing power, its results swing with copper prices, and at about 30x trailing earnings there is no margin of safety. A controlling shareholder owning 88.9% also limits the owner-oriented governance Buffett prefers.
summaries.munger: Munger would recognise the quality of the ore bodies and low costs, but he generally avoided commodity businesses whose fortunes depend on prices they cannot control, and the stock trades at a full price after a strong run. Inverting, the ways it could disappoint (copper price falls, Peruvian social conflict, Mexican policy changes) are real.
summaries.lynch: In Lynch's terms it is a cyclical, and he warned that cyclicals look cheapest at peak earnings; with copper near record levels and consensus expecting 2027 EPS to fall about 22%, this looks more like late-cycle than early-cycle. The story is simple (more copper from new mines in Peru and Mexico), but the P/E of about 30 is far above its expected growth.
summaries.fisher: Fisher prized companies with growing sales from new products, strong R&D and sales organisations; Southern Copper grows only by building new mines and spends little on research. Management is competent on costs and the project pipeline (Tia Maria, Los Chancas, Michiquillay) is long, but it does not fit Fisher's growth-company profile.
summaries.graham: It meets Graham's size, long profit record and long dividend history tests, and its balance sheet is sound, but at about 30x trailing earnings and about 13.8x book value it fails his price tests (P/E under 15 and P/E x P/B under 22.5) by a wide margin.
summaries.thiel: Copper mining is a competitive commodity market, not a monopoly built on proprietary technology; its only 'secret' is owning large, low-cost deposits. It fails most of Thiel's seven questions except durability of its resource position.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for durable growth at reasonable prices with disciplined management; Southern Copper offers high margins and an electrification tailwind but slow volume growth, revenue that follows copper prices, and a valuation of about 30x earnings with falling consensus 2027 estimates.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller trades liquidity and inflections; copper's surge has driven a strong share-price run and first-half 2026 net income up 69%, which fits his momentum and macro lens, but consensus already expects earnings to fall in 2027, so the next 18-24 months may look worse, not better.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith avoids cyclical commodity producers whose returns depend on prices they cannot control and which need heavy capital spending; despite high recent returns, Southern Copper does not meet his 'good company' test and is not cheap.
summaries.greenblatt: Return on capital is high at current copper prices, but the earnings yield is low: trailing operating income of about $9.0 billion against an enterprise value of about $175 billion is roughly 5%, so it would rank poorly on the Magic Formula's cheapness leg.
summaries.akre: Akre's stool needs a great business, talented and owner-like managers, and reinvestment at high returns; Southern Copper reinvests in high-return mines but is a price-taking commodity business with a new CEO and a controlling parent, so it fits only partly.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai wants heads-I-win, tails-I-don't-lose-much bets in distressed situations; Southern Copper is a quality low-cost miner but is priced near its highs after a copper boom, so there is no distress or margin of safety to exploit.
summaries.wood: It is not a disruptive-innovation company; it supplies copper that electric vehicles, grids and AI data centres need, but ARK-style platforms such as AI, robotics or energy storage are not its business.
summaries.ackman: Ackman favours simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with pricing power and limited exposure to outside forces; Southern Copper is simple and generates cash but is highly exposed to commodity prices and has a controlling shareholder that would block activism.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's 'scale economics shared' model, where a company passes savings to customers to grow, does not apply to a commodity miner that sells at market prices; its long-lived reserves are durable but its future depends on copper prices.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for huge markets with a technology-driven product; Southern Copper serves a huge copper market but with no new technology, so it does not fit a venture lens.
summaries.nash: Tom Nash explicitly avoids commodity producers, and Southern Copper also fails his kill test on more debt ($7,994.4m) than cash ($7,329.9m) at June 30, 2026, and on valuation, despite excellent margins and strong recent revenue growth. Its Nash-style score is about 55 of 130, well below the 75 bar.

momentum.evidence: The shares closed at $208.69 on Oct 12, 2026, near the top of a 52-week range of $115.69-$220.78, helped by copper averaging $6.04/lb in Q2 2026.

g4.evidence: It is backed by Grupo Mexico (88.9% owner, controlled by the Larrea family), but long-time CEO Oscar Gonzalez Rocha died in April 2026 and Leonardo Contreras Lerdo de Tejada took over on April 23, 2026.

g6.evidence: Several brokers have downgraded it (JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley to Underweight, UBS to Sell) with targets well below the share price, citing valuation.

simple.evidence: It mines and sells copper, molybdenum, silver and zinc from mines in Mexico and Peru; results mostly follow metal prices and volumes.

b2.evidence: It has been profitable every year from 2016 to 2025, but net income swung from $776.5m (2016) to $3,397.1m (2021), $2,425.2m (2023) and $4,334.9m (2025) with copper prices.

integrity.evidence: Reporting is straightforward and most profit is paid out as dividends, but Grupo Mexico's 88.9% control, related-party dealings and a CEO with no announced pay changes limit minority-holder alignment.

b6.evidence: It sticks to developing its own copper deposits (Tia Maria, Los Chancas, Michiquillay, El Pilar) rather than large acquisitions.

roic.evidence: 2025 operating income of $7,001.7m on SCC equity of about $12.6bn and net debt under $1bn implies very high returns, with modest leverage (interest coverage about 16.8x).

fcf.evidence: 2025 free cash flow was $3,426.8m (operating cash flow $4,752.1m less capex $1,325.3m), about 79% of net income of $4,334.9m, but capex is rising with a program it says exceeds $20.5bn this decade.

b10.evidence: It pays out most earnings (dividends paid $2,485.1m in 2025) and retained earnings funded growth projects, but output fell from 973,851 t in 2024 to 956,270 t in 2025, so value growth has come mostly from copper prices.

safety.evidence: At about 30x trailing EPS and about 13.8x book value, the price is well above a conservative value; a Nash-style DCF at 12% gives roughly $68 per share versus $208.69.

fairprice.evidence: About 29x 2026 consensus EPS of $7.23 and 37x 2027 consensus of $5.63 is expensive for a cyclical miner with expected falling earnings.

mu5.evidence: Low costs and large reserves make permanent failure unlikely, but copper price falls, Peruvian community opposition and Mexican mining-law changes could hurt it badly.

reinvest.evidence: It has a long project pipeline (Tia Maria 120,000 t/yr from 2H27 at an estimated $1.16/lb cash cost; Los Chancas; Michiquillay) that should earn good returns if copper prices hold.

ly2.evidence: It is a classic cyclical: profits rise and fall with the copper price, with a simple story of growing output toward 1.6 million tons by 2033.

ly3.evidence: A trailing P/E of about 30 is far above expected earnings growth; consensus sees 2027 EPS falling about 22%.

runway.evidence: It aims to lift copper output from 956,270 t in 2025 toward 1.6 million tons by 2033, but only by adding mines, not new products or regions.

ly7.evidence: It is not reducing its share count; quarterly stock dividends since 2024 have raised weighted shares from 795.3m (2023, restated) to 829.1m in Q2 2026.

ly8.evidence: Only about 11% of shares float because Grupo Mexico owns 88.9%, so coverage is thinner than for peers, but copper is a popular theme.

fi2.evidence: Its products (copper, molybdenum, silver, zinc) do not change; growth comes from new mines, not new products.

fi3.evidence: It reports no meaningful R&D; exploration spend was $52.8m in 2025.

fi4.evidence: It sells commodities at market prices; selling skill is not a source of advantage.

longterm.evidence: It is investing for decades-long projects such as Michiquillay (production expected 2032), but also pays out most earnings as dividends.

gr1.evidence: It had 2025 net sales of $13,420.0m and a market value of about $174bn.

ni10.evidence: SEC filings show positive net income attributable to SCC every year from 2016 ($776.5m) to 2025 ($4,334.9m).

gr4.evidence: It has paid cash dividends every year in its filings (e.g. $1,159.6m in 2020 and $2,485.1m in 2025), and dividend data providers list continuous payments since its 1996 listing.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $1.00 in 2016 to $5.24 in 2025 (the 2025 figure is on a stock-dividend-restated share basis).

gr6.evidence: At $208.69 the price is about 30x trailing EPS and far above 15x average earnings.

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 30 times P/B of about 13.8 is roughly 420, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: It has no proprietary technology; its edge is its ore bodies.

timing.evidence: Copper demand from electrification is strong and copper averaged $6.04/lb in Q2 2026, but buying a miner at record prices is late in the cycle.

th3.evidence: It holds about 4% of world mined copper (956,270 t of 23,000 thousand t in 2025), a small share of a large, established market.

team.evidence: Grupo Mexico has long experience running mines, but the company is in a leadership transition after its CEO died in April 2026.

th5.evidence: It sells to traders and fabricators through annual contracts and spot sales; reaching customers is easy in a liquid commodity market.

durable.evidence: Large reserves (it says the world's largest copper reserves) and low costs should keep it a top producer for decades; copper has no obvious substitute in wiring at scale.

th7.evidence: Its opportunities (more copper for electrification) are widely recognised by all major miners.

trend.evidence: It benefits from electrification, grids and data-centre demand for copper, but as a raw-material supplier rather than a leader of the trend.

dr1.evidence: First-half 2026 net income rose to $3,246.8m from $1,919.4m, but consensus 2027 EPS of $5.63 is below 2026's $7.23.

dr2.evidence: Tia Maria (42% complete at June 30, 2026, start-up expected 2H27) will add volume, but consensus expects lower revenue in 2027.

dr4.evidence: A weaker dollar and lower rates usually support copper prices, but a slowdown in China or the global economy would hurt demand.

dr6.evidence: Tia Maria start-up in 2H27, El Pilar in 2H29 and higher copper prices are identifiable catalysts.

dr7.evidence: Commodity exposure, a controlling shareholder and a high valuation make it unsuitable as a large concentrated position for most investors.

gm.evidence: 2025 gross margin after depreciation was about 53.6% (net sales $13,420.0m less cost of sales $5,359.2m and DD&A $868.4m), very high for a miner, though it reflects low costs, not pricing power.

fcfyield.evidence: 2025 free cash flow of $3,426.8m against a market value of about $174bn is a yield of about 2.0%, low for a cyclical commodity producer.

gb2.evidence: Trailing operating income of about $8,983m against an enterprise value of about $175bn is an earnings yield of about 5%.

pa2.evidence: The business is near a cyclical high, not in a temporary setback.

pa4.evidence: Low costs and modest net debt limit business risk, but buying at about 30x peak-cycle earnings risks a large share-price fall if copper drops.

wo1.evidence: It is a copper miner, not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or sequencing.

wo2.evidence: Unit costs depend on ore grades and by-product prices; cash cost before by-products was about 229.7 cents/lb in the first half of 2026, not falling rapidly.

wo4.evidence: USGS reports world copper mine production flat at about 23,000 thousand t in 2024 and 2025; the market will not multiply in five years.

ns4.evidence: If Tia Maria, Los Chancas and Michiquillay are built, output could rise toward 1.6 million tons by 2033, but social and political risks in Peru make this uncertain.

va2.evidence: It supplies a critical material for electrification, but it is a commodity input rather than a solution to a specific customer pain.

tn1.evidence: Copper is an infrastructure input for the energy and AI build-out, but Southern Copper is a long-established miner, not a company built for that trend.

tn2.evidence: The market sees it as a copper miner, which is what it is.

tn3.evidence: It is a commodity producer, a zone Nash says to avoid.

tn4.evidence: It is very profitable and revenue grew in 2024 and 2025, but debt of $7,994.4m exceeded cash and investments of $7,329.9m at June 30, 2026, and revenue fell in 2022 and 2023.

tn9.evidence: It hits the instant kill of more debt ($7,994.4m) than cash and short-term investments ($7,329.9m) at June 30, 2026.

tn18.evidence: The CEO has been in the role only since April 23, 2026 and is not a founder; no open-market purchases are known.

tn20.evidence: Results swing with metal prices; a consistent record of beating consensus could not be verified from primary sources.

tn22.evidence: It has $13,420.0m of 2025 revenue, $4,334.9m of net income, and issues no shares for cash (stock dividends aside).

tn24.evidence: A $174bn market value with a roughly 2% free-cash-flow yield implies sustained double-digit growth, above the company's planned volume growth of roughly 6% a year to 2033.

tn25.evidence: Using 3-year averages (revenue growth about 10.5%, FCF margin about 27%) from 2025 FCF of $3,426.8m, 4% terminal growth and a 12% discount rate gives about $68 per share versus $208.69.
